diagnostic.question: Which of the following best describes the stored-program (Von Neumann) concept that underlies most modern computers?
diagnostic.optionA: Programs must be physically rewired into the hardware for each new task
diagnostic.optionB: Both program instructions and data are stored in the same memory and can be fetched and modified like any other data
diagnostic.optionC: Instructions are permanently etched onto read-only chips and cannot be changed
diagnostic.optionD: Each instruction requires a separate dedicated processor

diagnostic.question: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1011?
Which logic gate outputs 1 only when all of its inputs are 1?
Which CPU component performs arithmetic and logical operations such as addition and comparison?
What is the primary purpose of an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)?
diagnostic.optionA: To define the physical layout of transistors on a chip
diagnostic.optionB: To define the set of instructions, registers, and data types that software can use to interact with the hardware
diagnostic.optionD: To define the operating system's file structure

diagnostic.question: Why do computer systems use a memory hierarchy (registers -> cache -> RAM -> disk) instead of a single type of memory?
diagnostic.optionA: Because a single memory technology cannot simultaneously provide high speed, large capacity, and low cost, so the hierarchy balances these tradeoffs
diagnostic.optionB: Because all memory types are equally fast and this is just a tradition
diagnostic.optionC: Because programs cannot run without multiple memory types
diagnostic.optionD: Because the operating system requires at least four separate memories to boot

diagnostic.question: What is the primary purpose of cache memory in a computer system?
diagnostic.optionA: To permanently store all program data
diagnostic.optionB: To provide a small, fast memory that holds frequently or recently used data, reducing average memory access time
diagnostic.optionC: To replace the need for a hard disk

diagnostic.question: Which I/O technique requires the CPU to continuously check (poll) a status flag to determine if an I/O device is ready, wasting CPU cycles while waiting?
What is the primary goal of instruction pipelining in CPU design?
diagnostic.optionA: To execute only one instruction per program run
diagnostic.optionB: To overlap the execution of multiple instructions in different stages, increasing instruction throughput
diagnostic.optionC: To eliminate the need for registers
diagnostic.optionD: To slow down the clock for safety

diagnostic.question: Which formula correctly relates CPU execution time to instruction count, clock cycles per instruction (CPI), and clock cycle time?
diagnostic.optionA: CPU time = Instruction count / (CPI x Clock cycle time)
diagnostic.optionB: CPU time = Instruction count x CPI x Clock cycle time
diagnostic.optionC: CPU time = Clock cycle time / (Instruction count x CPI)

practice.question: What are the three main functional components connected by buses in a basic computer system?
practice.explanation: The classic model (CPU, Memory, I/O) connected via address/data/control buses is the foundation of computer organization taught in every intro CA course.

practice.question: Which phase of the instruction cycle is responsible for determining what operation the instruction specifies?
practice.explanation: The decode phase interprets the opcode fetched from memory to determine the operation and operands required.

practice.question: What does the Program Counter (PC) hold?

options.text: The result of the last ALU operation
The address of the next instruction to execute

practice.explanation: The PC always points to the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched, and is updated (usually incremented) after each fetch.

practice.question: Which statement about the control bus is correct?

options.text: It carries only numeric operand values
It carries signals that indicate the type of operation (read/write/interrupt, etc.) being performed on the bus
It is only used during interrupts
It replaces the need for an address bus

practice.explanation: The control bus carries command/timing signals (such as memory read/write) that coordinate how the address and data buses are being used.

practice.question: A computer architecture defines the instruction set and registers visible to assembly programmers, while computer organization refers to:

options.text: How the hardware actually implements those architectural features (e.g. pipelining, cache design)

practice.explanation: Organization concerns the operational, hardware-level implementation of the architecture's programmer-visible contract.

practice.question: Convert the hexadecimal number 2F to decimal.
What is the 8-bit two's complement representation of -5?
practice.explanation: 5 = 00000101; invert to get 11111010; add 1 to get the two's complement: 11111011.

practice.question: In IEEE 754 single precision floating point, how many bits are allocated to the exponent field?
practice.explanation: Single precision uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 mantissa bits (total 32 bits).

practice.question: What is the result of adding binary 0110 and 0101 (4-bit, unsigned)?
practice.explanation: 0110 (6) + 0101 (5) = 11 = 1011 in binary, which fits exactly in 4 bits with no overflow.

practice.question: Which number system is most directly used for grouping binary digits in sets of three for human-readable representation?
practice.explanation: Each octal digit corresponds to exactly 3 binary bits, making octal a natural grouping of binary digits in threes.

practice.question: What is the output of a NOT gate when the input is 1?
practice.explanation: A NOT gate inverts its input, so an input of 1 produces an output of 0.

practice.question: Which gate is known as a 'universal gate' because any Boolean function can be implemented using only that gate?
practice.explanation: NAND (and also NOR) is functionally complete - any Boolean function, including NOT, AND, and OR, can be built using only NAND gates.

practice.question: According to De Morgan's theorem, NOT(A AND B) is equivalent to:
practice.explanation: De Morgan's theorem states NOT(A.B) = (NOT A) + (NOT B).

practice.question: What does a half-adder circuit compute?

options.text: The sum and carry of two single bits

practice.explanation: A half-adder takes two single-bit inputs and produces a Sum (XOR) and a Carry (AND) output.

practice.question: In Boolean algebra, what is the result of A + 1 (A OR 1) for any value of A?
practice.explanation: By the null/dominance law, ORing anything with 1 always yields 1, regardless of A.

practice.question: Which register holds the instruction currently being executed?
practice.explanation: The Instruction Register holds the instruction most recently fetched, so the control unit can decode it.

practice.question: What is the primary role of the Control Unit in a CPU?

options.text: Generating control signals that coordinate the operation of other CPU components

practice.explanation: The Control Unit does not perform computations itself; it orchestrates the other units by generating timing and control signals.

practice.question: A hardwired control unit implements control signals using:

options.text: A microprogram stored in control memory

practice.explanation: Hardwired control units use fixed combinational/sequential logic circuits rather than stored microinstructions.

practice.question: In a microprogrammed control unit, control signals are generated by:

options.text: Reading sequences of microinstructions stored in a control store/memory

practice.explanation: Microprogrammed control units store sequences of microinstructions, each asserting the control signals needed for one micro-step.

practice.question: What does the 'datapath' of a CPU refer to?

options.text: The set of functional units (registers, ALU, buses) and their interconnections that move and process data within the CPU

practice.explanation: The datapath is the collection of registers, ALU, and buses, and how they are wired together to move and transform data.

practice.question: In a 'three-address' instruction format, how many operands does a typical instruction specify?
practice.explanation: A three-address format names up to three operands explicitly, typically two sources and one destination.

practice.question: What does 'immediate addressing mode' mean?

options.text: The operand value itself is embedded directly in the instruction
The operand is in a register

practice.explanation: In immediate addressing, the constant value to be used is encoded directly within the instruction, needing no further memory access.

practice.question: Which addressing mode uses a register to directly hold the operand's value?
practice.explanation: Register addressing specifies a register that directly contains the operand value itself.

practice.question: Which of the following best characterizes a RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) design philosophy?

options.text: A small set of simple, fixed-length instructions that typically execute in one cycle

practice.explanation: RISC designs favor a small, simple, uniform instruction set that is easy to pipeline and typically executes in one cycle per instruction.

practice.question: Which of these is an example of a CISC-style processor family?
practice.explanation: x86 is the classic example of a CISC instruction set, with many complex, variable-length instructions.

practice.question: Which level of the memory hierarchy is typically fastest but smallest in capacity?
practice.explanation: Registers sit at the very top of the hierarchy: fastest to access but smallest in number/capacity.

practice.question: What does 'temporal locality' refer to?

options.text: Recently accessed memory locations are likely to be accessed again soon
Nearby memory locations are likely to be accessed soon
Memory access time depends on temperature
All memory accesses take the same time

practice.explanation: Temporal locality is the tendency to reuse recently accessed data/instructions again in the near future.

practice.question: What does 'spatial locality' refer to?

options.text: Recently used data will be reused
Memory locations near a recently accessed address are likely to be accessed soon
Memory is organized spatially on a chip

practice.explanation: Spatial locality is the tendency for programs to access memory locations near recently accessed ones (e.g. sequential array traversal).

practice.question: Which of these is an example of secondary memory?
practice.explanation: Hard disks and SSDs are classic secondary (persistent, non-volatile) storage, distinct from primary memory like RAM.

practice.question: As you move down the memory hierarchy (registers -> cache -> RAM -> disk), what generally happens to capacity and access time?

options.text: Capacity increases, access time increases (gets slower)

practice.explanation: Lower hierarchy levels trade speed for much larger capacity and lower cost per byte.

practice.question: In direct-mapped cache, each main memory block maps to:
practice.explanation: Direct mapping uses a fixed function of the block's address to determine the single line it must occupy.

practice.question: In a fully associative cache, a memory block can be placed:
practice.explanation: Fully associative caches allow a block to be placed in any line, maximizing placement flexibility.

practice.question: What is a 'cache hit'?

options.text: When requested data is NOT found in the cache
When requested data IS found in the cache

practice.explanation: A hit occurs whenever the requested data is already present in the cache.

practice.question: Which cache replacement policy evicts the block that has not been used for the longest time?
practice.explanation: LRU specifically tracks recency of use and evicts whichever block was used longest ago.

practice.question: What is the difference between a write-through and write-back cache policy?

options.text: Write-through writes to cache and main memory simultaneously on every write; write-back only writes to main memory later, when the block is evicted

practice.explanation: Write-through keeps memory always current at the cost of more traffic; write-back defers memory updates until eviction, reducing traffic but requiring dirty-bit tracking.

practice.question: Given the write-back policy from the previous question, what additional hardware bit does each cache line need to track whether it must be written back to memory before eviction?
practice.explanation: The dirty bit marks whether a cache line has been modified since being loaded; only dirty lines need to be written back to main memory on eviction under a write-back policy.

practice.question: In interrupt-driven I/O, what happens when a device becomes ready?

options.text: The device sends an interrupt signal to the CPU, which then stops its current task to service the request
The device directly accesses memory without CPU involvement

practice.explanation: Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device itself signals readiness via an interrupt.

practice.question: What is the main advantage of Direct Memory Access (DMA) over interrupt-driven I/O for large data transfers?

options.text: DMA requires the CPU to copy every byte
DMA allows a device to transfer data directly to/from memory with minimal CPU intervention, freeing the CPU for other tasks
DMA is slower than programmed I/O
DMA eliminates the need for memory

practice.explanation: DMA offloads the repetitive work of moving large blocks of data from the CPU to a dedicated controller.

practice.question: What is 'bus arbitration'?

options.text: The process of deciding which device gets to use the shared bus when multiple devices request it simultaneously
A method of encrypting data on the bus
A type of cache replacement policy
The physical layout of bus wires

practice.explanation: Arbitration resolves contention among multiple devices wanting simultaneous access to a shared bus.

practice.question: Memory-mapped I/O means that:

options.text: I/O devices are assigned addresses within the same address space as memory, so the CPU can access them using ordinary load/store instructions
I/O devices have their own completely separate CPU
Only disk devices can be accessed this way

practice.explanation: Memory-mapped I/O folds device registers into the regular memory address space, letting normal load/store instructions address them.

practice.question: In isolated I/O (separate I/O address space), accessing I/O devices requires:

options.text: Special dedicated I/O instructions (e.g. IN/OUT) distinct from memory instructions

practice.explanation: Isolated I/O keeps a distinct address space for devices, requiring special instructions rather than ordinary memory instructions.

practice.question: In the classic 5-stage RISC pipeline (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback), how many instructions can be in different stages simultaneously, ideally?
practice.explanation: Ideally, one instruction can occupy each of the 5 stages at once, giving 5 instructions in flight simultaneously.

practice.question: What is a 'structural hazard' in pipelining?

options.text: When two or more instructions need to use the same hardware resource (e.g. a single memory port) at the same time

practice.explanation: Structural hazards arise from limited hardware resources being needed by more than one in-flight instruction simultaneously.

practice.question: What is a 'data hazard'?

options.text: When an instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction that hasn't completed yet

practice.explanation: Data hazards occur when an instruction needs a value that an earlier, still-in-flight instruction has not yet produced.

practice.question: What is a 'control hazard' (branch hazard)?

options.text: A conflict over register file ports
Uncertainty about which instruction to fetch next due to a pending branch decision

practice.explanation: Control hazards stem from not yet knowing a branch's outcome/target, creating uncertainty about which instruction to fetch next.

practice.question: Which pipeline hazard-resolution technique forwards a computed result directly from one pipeline stage to an earlier stage that needs it, without waiting for it to be written back to the register file?
practice.explanation: Forwarding (bypassing) routes a result directly to where it is needed, skipping the wait for a formal register-file writeback.

practice.question: Given that data forwarding resolves many data hazards without stalling, what type of data hazard can forwarding alone NOT resolve, requiring a pipeline stall instead?

options.text: A RAW hazard where the needed value is produced early enough to forward
A load-use hazard where the dependent instruction needs a value that only becomes available after the Memory stage, later than forwarding paths can deliver it in time
A hazard that does not exist in any real pipeline
A WAW hazard in a simple 5-stage non-reordering pipeline

practice.explanation: When a LOAD instruction's result is needed by the very next instruction, the value isn't available until the Memory stage completes - later than ALU-to-ALU forwarding paths can supply it - so the pipeline must stall (insert a bubble) for one cycle even with forwarding hardware in place.

practice.question: What does 'CPI' stand for in CPU performance analysis?
practice.explanation: CPI (Cycles Per Instruction) is the average number of clock cycles needed to execute one instruction.

practice.question: According to Amdahl's Law, the maximum possible speedup from parallelizing part of a program is fundamentally limited by:

options.text: The number of processor cores available only
The fraction of the program that must remain serial (cannot be parallelized)

practice.explanation: Amdahl's Law shows the serial (non-parallelizable) fraction sets a hard ceiling on achievable speedup, regardless of how many processors are added.

practice.question: What does 'MIPS' (Million Instructions Per Second) measure?

options.text: A raw rate of instruction execution, often used (with caveats) as a performance metric

practice.explanation: MIPS measures how many instructions execute per second, though it can be misleading when comparing different instruction sets.

practice.question: In Flynn's taxonomy, which classification describes a system with a single instruction stream applied simultaneously to multiple data streams?
practice.explanation: SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) applies one instruction stream across many data elements at once, as in vector processors or GPUs.

practice.question: In Flynn's taxonomy, MIMD (Multiple Instruction, Multiple Data) best describes:

options.text: Modern multicore/multiprocessor systems where independent processors execute different instructions on different data concurrently
A GPU executing one instruction across many data elements

practice.explanation: MIMD systems have multiple independent processors, each executing its own instruction stream on its own data - the model for most modern multicore/multiprocessor systems.
